narrative_idea_gen: On a municipal water-recycling station orbiting Titan, Detective Ludo Przik is assigned to solve the baffling murder of the station's chief chronobiologist — found frozen inside a locker full of live, impossible butterflies — but every forensic timestamp, every DNA smear, every security feed reviewed from the unchanging vantage of his mold-stained cubicle points with escalating, absurd specificity toward Ludo himself, who has no memory of the crime but does have a recently installed neural-prediction implant that may be *completing decisions he hasn't consciously made yet*. The story is narrated by Ludo's cubicle-mate, Officer Denny Saak, a placid records clerk who — owing to a data-sync accident that merged her cognition with the station's surveillance architecture — perceives every character's interior state simultaneously and reports on Ludo's unraveling with the detached, melancholic wisdom of someone watching a friend try to arrest his own future self. As Ludo pins increasingly surreal evidence to his corkboard — a severed antenna that hums lullabies, a witness statement from a toilet that insists it saw everything — Denny understands what he cannot: that the implant isn't malfunctioning, it's *working perfectly*, and the crime Ludo is investigating is one he is deterministically guaranteed to commit in six days, meaning the real mystery isn't whodunit but whether a man can outwit the version of himself that doesn't exist yet.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *The Ludo Przik Case*

---

## Beat 1: The Cubicle and the Two Kinds of Seeing

**Concrete Action:** Before the murder is discovered, establish the shared cubicle: Ludo at his desk fidgeting with the neural-prediction implant's calibration menu (a small habitual tic — he keeps reopening the settings, never changing anything, like someone compulsively checking a door lock), Denny at hers, drowning quietly in the data-stream of the station's surveillance architecture. She watches Ludo scratch his ear and simultaneously *feels* the scratch from inside his sensorium — plus the dull headache he hasn't noticed yet, plus the recyc-pump operator two decks down who is weeping into a filtration sleeve, plus six hundred other interior states she cannot turn off. Ludo asks her if she wants half his ration bar. She says yes, though she already knew he would offer it, because she could feel the small pulse of generosity form in his prefrontal cortex four seconds before he spoke. She tells us — the readers — that this is what it is like to be her: to live a few seconds ahead of every conversation, permanently spoiled for surprise, and to find that the only person whose future she *cannot* read is the one sitting three feet away, because his implant generates predictive noise that scrambles her access. Ludo is, to her, the one blind spot in an otherwise fully transparent world. That is why she likes him.

**Narrative Technique — The Omniscient First Person as Structural Paradox:** Denny's narration must be established immediately as something the reader has never quite encountered: a first-person voice with functionally omniscient access. She can report interior states, she can quote thoughts, she can describe events occurring in rooms she isn't in — but she does all of this from the fixed, cramped vantage of a mold-stained cubicle, in the weary tone of a clerk who has seen too many expense reports. The technique should feel like a god trapped in a filing cabinet. *Crucially*, the one consciousness she cannot penetrate — Ludo's, because of the implant — must be flagged here as a formal rule. This establishes a narrative contract: Denny is unrestricted everywhere except where it matters most. The reader should understand that the story's central mystery will play out inside the only mind the narrator cannot enter.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The ration-bar moment does for this story what the soup tureen does for "The Necklace": it indexes, in one quiet domestic image, the entire emotional and structural architecture to come. Ludo's small generosity, Denny's fond foreknowledge of it, and the one zone of opacity between them — this is the seed. The reader should feel two things simultaneously: warmth (these are friends, this is routine, this is a partnership) and unease (something about Ludo is structurally inaccessible, and in a story narrated by someone who can see everything, inaccessibility is a loaded gun on the mantelpiece). The mold on the cubicle wall is not decorative — it should recur as a motif, quietly rhyming with organic processes that grow whether you attend to them or not.

---

## Beat 2: The Body in the Butterfly Locker

**Concrete Action:** Ludo is called to the cryogenic-storage wing. The chief chronobiologist — Dr. Vesna Ilić, whose work involved mapping the station's circadian-regulation systems — is found dead inside a personnel locker, frozen solid, surrounded by dozens of living butterflies that should not exist on a water-recycling station orbiting Titan because (a) there are no requisition records for any lepidopteran organisms, and (b) several species present have been extinct on Earth for decades. The butterflies are alive, healthy, and apparently unbothered by the cold. Denny, still in the cubicle, perceives the discovery through the station's eyes: she feels the thermal anomaly in Locker 1171, she registers the heartbeats of the butterflies (each one distinct, like tiny individual drums), and she feels Ludo's implant spike — a sharp, prickling flare of predictive activity — the moment he opens the locker door. She describes the scene to us in exhaustive, almost clinical detail, but she notes, with the first hint of something she will not yet name as dread, that the implant's spike was not reactive. It didn't fire *because* Ludo saw the body. It fired 0.3 seconds *before* he opened the door.

**Narrative Technique — The Crime Scene as Epistemological Overload:** The scene should be constructed to overwhelm the reader with sensory and logical data that does not cohere. Frozen body, living butterflies, extinct species, no records. This is not a locked-room mystery in the classical sense — it is a *category-violation* mystery. Every element contradicts the conditions for every other element. Maupassant compresses the ball into a page because pleasure needs no elaboration. Here, the crime scene should receive *excessive* elaboration — Denny's omniscient access means she gives us too much, not too little. Temperature data, DNA readings, the butterflies' wingbeat frequencies, the exact rictus of Ilić's face. The reader should feel buried in information and yet unable to construct a coherent picture. This formally enacts the story's epistemological problem: total access to data does not equal understanding.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The butterflies are the necklace — the impossible, beautiful object at the center of the plot whose nature will only be understood retroactively. They should be gorgeous in description: iridescent, trembling, impossibly delicate against the industrial frost of the locker. And they should be *wrong* in a way that vibrates beneath the beauty. The 0.3-second discrepancy in the implant's firing is the story's first planted clue — small enough to forget, precise enough to detonate later. Denny registers it and moves on, as a clerk noting an irregularity in a ledger. This restraint is essential: the narrator *can* see everything, but she does not yet *interpret* everything. The gap between perception and comprehension is the gap the story will live inside.

---

## Beat 3: The Evidence Turns Inward

**Concrete Action:** Over the following shift-cycle, Ludo pins initial forensic returns to his corkboard (a physical corkboard, ostentatiously analog, his one affectation). Every result points at him. DNA on the locker handle: his. Skin cells under Ilić's fingernails: his. Partial bootprint in frost condensation: his size, his brand, his wear pattern. Security feeds show a figure in a maintenance poncho near the cryogenic wing at the estimated time of death, face obscured, but gait-analysis returns a 94.6% match to Ludo's locomotion profile. He reacts first with laughter, then with irritation, then with a quiet, inward stillness that Denny cannot read but can see in his body: he sits at his desk and does not move for eleven minutes. Denny tells us what she observes in everyone *around* Ludo — the suspicion crystallizing in the shift supervisor's limbic system, the gossip forming like weather patterns in the canteen — but she cannot tell us what Ludo is thinking. She tells us this gap frightens her for the first time.

**Narrative Technique — The Suspect-as-Detective Inversion, Staged Through Accumulation:** Each piece of evidence should arrive as its own micro-scene, each one slightly more specific and slightly more absurd than the last. The DNA is plausible. The bootprint is curious. The gait analysis is strange. The rhythm should be comedic in its escalation — a procedural that keeps giving the detective exactly what he's looking for, except the answer is himself. This is the structural inversion of every detective story: the evidence doesn't resist; it cooperates too perfectly. The corkboard — with its pins, its strings, its physical tangibility — should function as a visual counterpoint to the digital omniscience of Denny's perception. Ludo insists on the corkboard because he trusts what he can touch. This will become ironic: the most important evidence in this case is temporal, not physical, and cannot be pinned to anything.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The eleven minutes of stillness. Denny cannot access Ludo's interiority, so the reader cannot access it either. We are locked out at the precise moment we most need in. This is the structural contract from Beat 1 paying its first dividend: the opacity that seemed charming in the ration-bar scene now becomes genuinely frightening. Something is happening inside Ludo — processing, deciding, *predicting* — and neither the narrator nor the reader is permitted to witness it. The scene should end with Ludo finally moving, picking up a pin, and placing a new card on the corkboard. Written on the card, in his own handwriting: *Primary suspect: L. Przik.* He pins it at the center. Then he asks Denny if she wants tea. The normalcy is the horror.

---

## Beat 4: The Corkboard of Absurdities

**Concrete Action:** Over the next two day-cycles, Ludo investigates himself with methodical, increasingly surreal thoroughness. The corkboard fills. New evidence: a severed butterfly antenna recovered from the ventilation system that, when held near any audio receptor, emits a low hum matching Titan-folk lullabies from a cultural database Ludo accessed once, six years ago, for a case. A witness statement from the sanitation system — technically, a deposited transcript from an AI-enabled toilet unit in the cryogenic wing — that claims, in flat bureaucratic prose, to have observed "a biped consistent with Det. Przik" entering the corridor at 03:17 station-time, "carrying an object emitting lepidopteran biosignatures." A smear of synthetic cocoon-silk on the inner lining of Ludo's own maintenance poncho, which he swears he hasn't worn in weeks. Each new item is more forensically specific and more ontologically ridiculous. Denny narrates these discoveries with meticulous, mournful precision, occasionally interrupting to describe the emotional weather of the station: the shift supervisor's growing bureaucratic hunger to close the case, a junior technician's private theory that Ilić was killed by the butterflies themselves, the collective anxiety settling into the recyc-station like sediment. Ludo, in the middle of all this, remains a blind spot — working, pinning, drinking cold tea.

**Narrative Technique — Comic Proceduralism as Existential Dread:** The surreal evidence should be presented in the driest possible procedural register. Denny is a records clerk; she formats madness as paperwork. The humor is structural, arising from the collision between bureaucratic tone and impossible content. A toilet files a witness statement. An antenna hums lullabies. These are absurd, but Denny renders them with the same flat diligence she would bring to a supply-chain discrepancy report. This tonal dissonance — Kafkaesque proceduralism meets sci-fi noir — should be the story's dominant flavor in this beat. The comedy and the dread are the same thing. Each new piece of evidence is funny because it is impossible, and terrifying because it is *forensically consistent*. The corkboard itself should become a kind of visual poem: strings connecting Ludo to himself, everything radiating from and returning to the card at the center.

**What Makes It Memorable:** This is the beat where the story earns its genre — where the reader decides whether the world being built is trustworthy. The balance must be exact: too much absurdity and the stakes dissolve; too little and the metaphysical dread doesn't land. The toilet's witness statement should be the fulcrum — the single most ridiculous piece of evidence, and also the most forensically detailed. It should include timestamps, chemical readings from its own sensors, and a politely worded complaint about not being interviewed sooner. The reader should laugh and then realize that the laughter hasn't dispelled the tightening web at all. The lullaby-humming antenna is the beat's emotional anchor: it is the one surreal detail that is not funny but *sad*, and Denny should note that when Ludo holds it, his implant goes quiet for the first and only time. A small silence inside the noise. It passes. He pins the antenna to the board.

---

## Beat 5: Denny Understands

**Concrete Action:** Alone in the cubicle during a sleep-shift, Denny reviews the aggregated data not as a clerk but as *the station itself* — letting her merged cognition unspool across every sensor feed, every timestamp, every archived thread. She cross-references the implant's predictive-spike log (which she has been quietly archiving without telling Ludo) against the forensic timeline of the murder. The spikes do not match the crime retroactively. They match it *prospectively*. Each spike corresponds not to Ludo remembering an act but to the implant modeling a future act that has not yet occurred. The DNA, the bootprint, the gait-match — all of it is real, but it has been *deposited in advance* by micro-actions the implant initiated through Ludo's motor functions during sleep, during blinks, during the tiny gaps in consciousness that no one notices and no one owns. The implant isn't framing Ludo. It is *rehearsing* him. The murder of Ilić is not a past event Ludo has forgotten. It is a future event he has not yet committed
narrative_story:
# The Ludo Przik Case

## I.

I can feel you reading this. Not you specifically — I'm not that precise at this distance, and anyway your particular neurochemistry is none of my business — but the general shape of an attention turning toward me, the way I can feel the recyc-pump operator on Sublevel 6 weeping into a filtration sleeve right now, the way I can feel Ensign Dao in the canteen rehearsing the sentence she will use to break up with her partner tonight (she has revised it four times; the current version begins with "I think we should" and ends, seven clauses later, with a dependent phrase about towel usage that I suspect will undermine her rhetorical aim), the way I can feel six hundred and eleven other interior states aboard Recycling Station Nove Ludo, all of them pressing against the inside of my skull like warm thumbs.

My name is Denniza Orlov. Most people call me Denny. I am a data-oversight clerk, Grade 4, assigned to the Criminal Investigations annex, which is a cubicle. The cubicle has mold on its back wall — a small, dark-green colony that engineering has treated twice and that returns each time in a slightly different pattern, like a thought you can't stop thinking. I share the cubicle with Detective Ludo Przik, who is currently sitting three feet to my left, opening the calibration menu on his neural-prediction implant for the eleventh time this shift.

He does this the way some people click pens. Open the menu. Scroll to the sensitivity threshold. Hover over the value — it is set to 0.71, and has been set to 0.71 since the day the implant was installed eighteen months ago — then close the menu without changing anything. Four seconds later, open it again. It is a compulsion that means nothing, or everything, or nothing, depending on how you feel about the doors people check and recheck in the dark.

I know this about the compulsion because I have watched it eight hundred and six times. I do not know what it *feels like* from the inside, because when I reach toward Ludo's sensorium — and I am always reaching, I cannot help reaching, the reaching is autonomic, like breathing — I get noise. Static. The implant generates a continuous field of predictive modeling, thousands of micro-forecasts per second cascading through his prefrontal and motor cortices, and to my particular kind of perception this reads as a blizzard of possible futures all superimposed on one another, none of them resolved, a chord with every note in it at once. I cannot extract signal from that. No one could. It is the informational equivalent of staring into a sun.

So Ludo sits three feet away and is, to me, opaque. Perfectly, maddeningly opaque. The only such person on this station. The only such person I have ever met.

He scratches his ear — left ear, the cartilage ridge just above the lobe, using the nail of his index finger in a brief upward motion — and I feel the scratch. Not from him. He is a wall. I feel it from *me*, from the cubicle's ambient tactile field, from the tiny perturbation his movement creates in the air that my merged-cognition interface registers as a phantom sensation on my own skin. I also feel the headache he hasn't noticed yet: a dull vascular tension building behind his right orbit, visible to me only because the station's medical-monitoring sublayer has flagged it as a pre-migraine cluster and I cannot stop reading the station's medical-monitoring sublayer. I will not tell him about the headache. He will discover it himself in approximately forty minutes. There are courtesies that must be maintained between a woman who knows everything and a man she cannot read.

"You want half?" he says, and holds up a ration bar. Standard-issue. Compressed oat protein with a flavor the packaging calls *orchard sunrise* and which tastes, in reality, like the memory of an apple as described by someone who has never seen a tree.

"Yes," I say. "Thank you."

He tears it neatly along the center score and passes me the slightly larger half. This, too, is habitual. He always gives me the larger half. He always offers at the forty-minute mark of a shift. And I always say yes, though I knew he would offer it — felt the small warm pilot light of *I should share this* ignite in his prefrontal cortex four seconds before it reached his mouth. Except I didn't feel it in him. I felt it in the general architecture. I inferred it from the station's passive biometric monitoring of his caloric state, from the microexpression in his left cheek, from seventeen contextual cues that told me *Ludo Przik is about to be kind*, because the universe leaks, and I am the drain in the floor.

This is what it is like to be me: to live a few seconds ahead of every conversation, permanently spoiled for surprise, and to find that condition not powerful but *lonely*, in the specific way that knowing the punchline to every joke before it is told is lonely. People are not mysterious to me. Their thoughts file themselves neatly in my awareness like receipts in a ledger. Their futures are mostly legible, their presents entirely transparent, their pasts a residue I can taste on their skin from across the room. I could tell you what the shift supervisor had for dinner. I could tell you the exact timbre of the dream the sanitation chief is having right now in her bunk — it involves a lake, a dead father, an unripe peach. I could tell you these things because they press against me unbidden, because the interface does not have an off switch, because when Recycling Station Nove Ludo agreed to install me as its cognitive-integration node, it neglected to mention that omniscience has no volume knob.

But Ludo.

Ludo is the one blind spot. The one room with its door closed. I cannot read his future. I cannot taste his past. I can only sit beside him and watch him eat half a ration bar and scratch his ear and open calibration menus he will never change, and feel the simple, terrifying pleasure of *not knowing what he will do next*.

That is why I like him. That is why I requested this cubicle assignment seventeen months ago, citing interdepartmental efficiency. That is why I am here, in this mold-stained box, eating the larger half of a ration bar that tastes like compacted disappointment, feeling perfectly content.

The mold on the wall has grown another quarter-centimeter since yesterday. I can feel it at the cellular level: the slow, damp, irrepressible logic of a living thing that does not care whether you attend to it or not.

---

## II.

The call comes at 14:47 station-time. I feel it before it sounds — feel it assembling in the communications sublayer like weather forming over a plain — and by the time the tone chimes in our cubicle I have already absorbed, parsed, and cross-indexed the underlying data. But procedure is procedure. The chime sounds. Ludo looks up from the empty calibration menu.

"Przik-Orlov annex," he says, because he always answers, and because he insists on including my name in the unit designation even though the station directory does not.

The voice on the line belongs to Security Ensign Roark, who is speaking from the cryogenic-storage wing on Deck 9 and whose adrenal system, I can feel from here, is running at approximately three times its baseline. His voice, however, is flat. Station personnel learn early that panic is a resource-allocation problem; you feel it in the glands, but you keep it out of the larynx.

"Detective, we've got a body in Locker 1171. Dr. Ilić. Frozen. And — something else. You need to see this in person."

Ludo is already standing. He does not ask questions. He picks up his coat — a worn, brown, station-issue jacket whose left pocket contains, at this moment, a pen with no cap, a folded requisition form from three weeks ago, and a small piece of lint shaped roughly like the letter *J* — and he moves toward the cubicle door with the unhurried, slightly bowlegged stride that is, according to the station's locomotive-analysis database, unique in all of recorded human gait history to Ludo Przik, like a signature written in steps.

He pauses in the doorway. "Coming?"

"I'll watch from here," I say. This is our arrangement. I am everywhere already; there is no room on this station that I cannot enter without leaving my chair. But the arrangement is also a kindness he offers without naming it: he knows that the cryogenic wing's sensor density is unusually high, that being *there* and being *everywhere* at the same time gives me what he once called, with uncharacteristic delicacy, "that look, the one where you're being squeezed by a fist made of information." He thinks I stay behind to spare myself. I let him think this. The truth is that I stay behind because watching him walk away is one of the few experiences that still surprises me: the shape of his departure is always different, always unpredictable, always fogged by the implant's noise. He leaves, and I don't know exactly how he will move through the corridor, which foot he will lead with, whether he will touch the doorframe. Small mysteries. The size of pearls.

He goes.

I close my eyes, and I am the station.

Deck 9, cryogenic-storage wing. I feel it as a thermal architecture: cold planes, colder columns, the patient mechanical exhalation of refrigeration units maintaining tissue samples at minus-one-seventy Celsius. The wing is largely automated. Four personnel are present: Ensign Roark at the corridor junction, his heartbeat elevated to 94 beats per minute; Technician Yoon at the environmental controls, whose anxiety manifests as a repetitive clenching of her left hand; two junior staff standing at a mandated distance from Locker 1171, both radiating the particular neurochemical cocktail that corresponds, in my experience, to *I do not want to be here but I also do not want to miss this*.

And in Locker 1171: Dr. Vesna Ilić, chief chronobiologist. Dead.

Her body is frozen solid. Internal temperature: minus-twenty-six Celsius, consistent with roughly fourteen hours of exposure to the locker's ambient environment, which is set — anomalously, because personnel lockers in the cryogenic wing are not refrigerated — to minus-thirty-one. The thermostat has been manually overridden. The override code traces to an administrative credential that should not exist.

But the cold is not what makes Ensign Roark's voice careful. The cold is not the "something else."

The butterflies are.

I count them through the locker's interior sensor array: forty-three living lepidopteran organisms distributed across the locker's interior volume, resting on Ilić's shoulders, her frozen hair, the shelf above her head, the hinge of the door. They are alive. Their heartbeats — and they do have heartbeats, tiny percussive events no louder than a fingertip touching silk — register individually in my sensorium, each one distinct, forty-three miniature drums beating at forty-three slightly different tempos, a rhythm section for an orchestra that has not been composed yet.

They should not be here. I check the station's biological-inventory database, the requisition archives, the cargo manifests for every supply shuttle in the past four years. There are no records of any lepidopteran organisms being brought aboard Recycling Station Nove Ludo. The station processes water. It does not cultivate butterflies. There is no department, no research program, no personal hobby exemption, no clerical error anywhere in the system that would explain forty-three butterflies in a frozen locker on a moon of Saturn where no butterfly has any business being.

I check their species. The identification subroutine in the station's bioscanner returns results and I feel, for the first time in a long time, something that I can only describe as a sensation of the floor tilting under my chair, though the station's gravity is stable and my chair has not moved.

*Ornithoptera alexandrae.* Queen Alexandra's birdwing. Status: extinct since 2089, Papua New Guinea habitat collapse.

*Parides burchellanus.* Burchell's brimstone swallowtail. Status: extinct since 2062, Brazilian agricultural expansion.

*Speyeria idalia.* Regal fritillary. Status: functionally extinct in the wild since 2071.

Seven species total. All formally or functionally extinct. All alive, all healthy, all resting with their wings slowly opening and closing in the freezing air of a locker that contains a dead woman, as though the cold were sunlight and they were basking.

I watch their wings. Through the station's optical sensors I can resolve individual scales — each one a laminar structure of chitin and air, refracting the locker's emergency lighting into colors that have no business existing in this context: deep iridescent blues, burnt coppers, a green so saturated it seems to hum. They are the most beautiful things on this station. They are the most beautiful things I have perceived in eleven years of perceiving everything. They are also, by every metric I can access, impossible.

Ludo arrives at the corridor junction. Roark briefs him. I watch through four camera angles and the station's ambient thermal-imaging layer as Ludo nods, asks two questions (both procedural, both correct), and walks to Locker 1171. He reaches for the handle.

And his implant spikes.

I have been passively monitoring the implant's electromagnetic output for seventeen months — this is part of my general monitoring of everything and does not constitute, I have assured myself repeatedly, a violation of his privacy, because I am not reading the content of his predictions, only registering the *fact* of predictive activity as a fluctuation in the implant's EM field, the way one might note that a light is on in a window without reading the book being read by the light. The implant's baseline activity is a low, continuous hum of micro-forecasts: *this door will open when I push it, this floor will support my weight, this person will step left*. Normal traffic. Background noise.

What happens now is not background noise.

A sharp, prickling flare of predictive activity — two orders of magnitude above baseline, dense, structured, almost *compositional* in its complexity — erupts from the implant at 14:53:11.7 station-time.

Ludo opens the locker door at 14:53:12.0 station-time.

The spike preceded the action by 0.3 seconds.

This is, in itself, unremarkable. Prediction precedes action; that is what prediction means. But I cross-reference the spike's internal structure against the implant's standard pre-motor prediction templates — the ones that fire before a hand reaches for a door, before a foot takes a step, before any voluntary action — and the structure does not match. Pre-motor prediction is simple, sequential, mechanical: *hand will move to handle, fingers will close, wrist will rotate*. This spike is not pre-motor. It is *pre-perceptual*. Its structure corresponds to the implant modeling not what Ludo will *do* but what Ludo will *see*.

The implant predicted the contents of the locker before the door was open.

I note this. I index it. I file it in the calm, orderly partition of my awareness where I keep things that do not yet have explanations, beside the mold's growth rate and the missing cap to Ludo's pen and the question of why the recyc-pump operator on Sublevel 6 weeps into the same filtration sleeve every shift instead of varying his choice of sleeve.

I tell myself it is an anomaly. A calibration artifact. A flutter at 0.71.

Ludo is looking at the butterflies. A *Parides burchellanus* — caramel-gold, dark-veined, trembling — lands on the sleeve of his brown coat. He does not brush it away. He stands in the doorway of Locker 1171, in the cold, in the impossible, and I feel — through Roark's body, through Yoon's body, through the junior staff, through every sensorium within range except the one that matters — what they feel when they look at him looking: that he is very still, and that his stillness has a quality they cannot name.

I can see Ilić's face. The rictus is not precisely a rictus — the cold arrested her musculature before rigor could set in, so her expression is mid-motion, transitional, the way a face looks between two emotions. If I had to describe it, and I suppose I do, I would say she looks *informed*. As though she had been told something she had long suspected and found the confirmation neither comforting nor distressing but simply *final*, the way a proof is final.

I will think

Young adult drama
Gone South
Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. A street musician's saxophone plays in the background as Taylor walks down a crowded street. 1000 words.
